planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring or fall in lean, sharply drained soil in full sun; established plants are drought tolerant and resent winter wet more than cold. CAUTION: the milky latex sap is a strong skin and eye irritant, so wear gloves and eye protection when cutting back old stems.

directions: This shrubby evergreen spurge forms a dense clump of upright stems clothed in narrow blue-gray leaves, topped in late winter and early spring by rounded chartreuse flower heads with a distinctive dark red-brown eye at the center of each true flower cluster. Each flowering stem is biennial, so cut spent stems back to the base at ground level after bloom to make room for the current season's new growth and keep the clump tidy. It thrives in poor, rocky, or sandy soil and full sun, needing little supplemental water once established, though it struggles in humid climates with heavy clay. Handle the cut stems and sap with gloves, since the latex is an irritant to skin and eyes and mildly toxic if ingested by pets or people.

common_name: Myrtle Spurge (Donkey Tail Spurge, Creeping Spurge)

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in lean, gritty, fast-draining soil in full sun; this species self-sows readily and is regulated as a noxious weed in parts of the western United States, so check local rules before planting and deadhead to limit spread.

directions: Myrtle spurge is a low, trailing succulent-leaved perennial with thick, prostrate stems radiating outward like spokes, each densely packed with fleshy, blue-gray, pointed leaves in an overlapping spiral. Clusters of chartreuse-yellow bracted flowers open at the stem tips in early spring, standing out against the icy foliage color. It is extremely drought and heat tolerant once rooted, thriving in rock gardens, gravel beds, and dry slopes with poor soil, but it self-sows aggressively and has escaped cultivation in several western states, where it is now listed as a noxious or invasive weed. Wear gloves when handling or trimming, since the milky sap is a significant skin and eye irritant, and deadhead spent flowers before seed drops to help keep the planting contained.
sources: King County Noxious Weed Control Program

planting.note: Plant container-grown perennials in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; established clumps resent being transplanted or divided, so choose a permanent spot. CAUTION: the milky sap is a skin and eye irritant, so wear gloves when cutting back the plant.

directions: Cushion spurge forms a neat, symmetrical dome of stems clothed in bright green leaves, smothered in early to mid spring with long-lasting acid-yellow bracts that make it a classic companion for spring bulbs. Foliage often takes on orange and red tones in fall before dying back for winter, adding a second season of color. It performs best in lean to average soil with excellent drainage and full sun, tolerating heat and drought well once established but declining in soggy or heavy clay sites. Shear the mound back by about half after flowering to maintain a tight habit and prevent legginess, wearing gloves since the cut stems exude an irritating milky latex typical of the genus.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in moisture-retentive soil in full sun to part shade; this cultivar spreads by rhizomes and can be vigorous, so give it room or a barrier. CAUTION: the milky sap is a skin and eye irritant, so wear gloves when dividing or cutting back stems.

directions: 'Fireglow' is an herbaceous, clump-forming spurge grown for its brilliant orange-red bracted flower heads in late spring and early summer, carried atop upright stems with narrow leaves marked by a pale midrib. Unlike many of its drought-tolerant relatives, this species prefers evenly moist, humus-rich soil and appreciates some afternoon shade in hot climates, making it a good choice for the front to middle of a mixed border. It spreads by creeping rhizomes to form an expanding colony over time and can be readily increased by digging and replanting rooted sections in spring. Wear gloves when dividing, deadheading, or cutting the plant back, since the cut stems exude a milky latex sap that is a notable skin and eye irritant and mildly toxic if ingested.
sources: Great Plant Picks (Elisabeth C. Miller Botanical Garden)
